beats.text: Paris, eighteen thirty-eight. A busy boulevard. Carriages, horses, people everywhere.
But in the very first photo of it, the street is empty.
The picture needed minutes of light. Everything that moved simply vanished. Except one man. He stood still, to get his boots shined.
That's how you got into a photo. You froze. Studios even put iron stands behind your head. Blink, and your face became a blur.
But by the eighteen fifties, it took just a few seconds.
So why still no smiles? A photo was rare, expensive, and forever. Some people were even told to say prunes, to keep the mouth small.
Then, in nineteen hundred, Kodak's Brownie camera cost one dollar. Suddenly, everyone took snapshots. And the smile moved in.
Today, your phone takes a photo in less than a hundredth of a second.
The street looked empty, because nobody stood still for minutes. You just need a blink.

sources: Daguerre, 'Boulevard du Temple' (1838): exposure of several minutes; moving traffic does not register; a man having his boots shined is the first person known to appear in a photograph. Sources: Getty/Smarthistory; Wikipedia 'Boulevard du Temple (photograph)'.

Early daguerreotype portraits (1839–1845) needed up to 60–90 s+; posing stands/head rests held sitters still; by the 1850s (faster lenses, collodion) a few seconds. Getty Museum (2023), 'Say Prunes! The surprising history of the smile in early photographs'; Mental Floss.
'Say prunes' to keep the mouth small: 19th-century advice cited by the Getty Museum article (2023).
Kodak Brownie: launched February 1900, price $1 (Kodak / George Eastman Museum). Phone exposure in normal light well under 1/100 s.
Film clips: Lumière, 'Paris, le Pont-Neuf' (1897) – illustrative, public domain (via Internet Archive).
